text: Pieter Willem Botha, DMS (locally /ˈbʊərtə/ BOOR-tə; Afrikaans pronunciation: [ˈpitər ˈvələm ˈbuəta]; 12 January 1916 – 31 October 2006), was a South African politician who served as the last Prime Minister of South Africa from 1978 to 1984 and as the first executive State President from 1984 until his resignation in 1989. Nicknamed 'Die Groot Krokodil' (Afrikaans for 'The Big Crocodile') due to his tough political stance, he was considered the final hardline leader of South Africa during the apartheid era. Born on 12 January 1916 on a small farm in the Paul Roux district of the Orange Free State Province (now Free State Province), Botha was the son of Afrikaner parents; his father, Pieter Willem Botha Sr., fought as a commando against the British in the Second Boer War, and his mother, Hendrina Christina Botha (née de Wet), was interned in a British concentration camp during that war. Raised in a conservative Afrikaner family with strong nationalist beliefs, Botha was influenced by Afrikaner culture and Calvinist religious teachings, emphasizing discipline, hard work, and loyalty to the Afrikaner cause. Growing up in the aftermath of the Second Boer War and amid rising Afrikaner nationalism, he internalized the belief that Afrikaners needed to assert political and economic control over South Africa. He initially attended the Paul Roux School and matriculated from Bethlehem Voortrekker High School. In 1934, he entered Grey University College (now the University of the Free State) in Bloemfontein to study law but left early at age twenty to pursue politics. He began working for the National Party as a political organizer in the neighbouring Cape Province, joined the Ossewabrandwag—an Afrikaner nationalist group sympathetic to the German Nazi Party—and helped found its Cape Town branch in 1939. After the German attack on the USSR, Botha condemned the Ossewabrandwag in August 1941, shifting to Christian nationalism and being expelled from the group. In 1943, he married Anna Elizabeth Rossouw (Elize), with whom he had five children: two sons (Piet and Rossouw) and three daughters (Elsa, Amelia, and Rozanne). In the 1980s, Rozanne emerged as a minor celebrity, releasing Afrikaans pop songs and appearing on magazine covers such as Sarie and Style, where she was dubbed "First Daughter of the Land." In 1998, he married Barbara Robertson, a legal secretary 25 years his junior, following Elize's death. In 2022, two of his daughters died: Amelia Paschke in a car crash driving back from Betty's Bay, and Rozanne from cancer. Botha was elected to parliament in 1948 as an MP for the National Party from George, coinciding with the party's rise to power under Prime Minister D.F. Malan, who formally instituted apartheid. As a staunch supporter of Afrikaner nationalism, he aligned with the baasskap faction, advocating for stricter racial policies and white minority rule. He gained a reputation for tough, uncompromising rhetoric, often warning of communist threats, black liberation movements, and international pressure, and displayed authoritarian tendencies by advocating for increased state power to suppress opposition. His main opponents in Parliament were Helen Suzman and Harry Schwarz, whom he frequently attacked. After retaining his seat in the 1953 and 1958 elections, he was appointed Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs by Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd, assisting in enforcing the Population Registration Act that classified all South Africans into four racial groups. In 1961, he became Minister of Community Development and Coloured Affairs, overseeing forced removals including the clearance of District Six. In 1966, he was appointed Minister of Defence by Prime Minister John Vorster, a role he held for over 15 years. As Defence Minister, he expanded the military, increased spending to 20% of the national budget from 1.3% in 1968, implemented conscription, launched covert operations against anti-apartheid movements, and initiated South Africa's nuclear weapons program under a doctrine of "strategic deterrence" to counter Soviet-backed forces in Southern Africa. He also established the policy of "total onslaught," framing racial policies as a Cold War struggle against communism and black liberation. The South African Defence Force (SADF) reached a peak under his leadership and was involved in the South African Border War. When Prime Minister John Vorster resigned in 1978 following allegations in the Muldergate Scandal, Botha was elected as his successor by the National Party caucus, defeating Foreign Minister Pik Botha and Connie Mulder in a 78–72 vote. On 5 December 1978, he was absolved of blame in the scandal. Upon becoming Prime Minister, he retained the defence portfolio until October 1980, when he appointed SADF Chief General Magnus Malan. He pursued an ambitious military policy to strengthen South Africa's military capabilities, sought improved relations with the West—especially the United States—but with mixed results, arguing that preserving the apartheid government was essential to countering African communism spreading into Angola and Mozambique after their independence. In one of his first moves, he appointed Piet Koornhof as minister responsible for black affairs, who later joined the ANC in the post-apartheid era and was regarded as one of the most reform-minded ministers. Botha led a campaign to demolish Crossroads, a high-density township in Cape Town in 1978, and later agreed with Koornhof to "indefinitely delay" the demolitions amid opposition. A challenge arose when Andries Treurnicht was elected leader of the Transvaal province, opposing apartheid reforms and holding a strong majority in the all-white parliament, highlighting differences between Afrikaners in Botha's Cape Province and Treurnicht's. In 1979, Botha became the first premier to visit Robben Island, declining to say if he met any prisoners, calling it a "routine" visit. In April 1979, he offered military and economic support to Abel Muzorewa's government in Zimbabwe Rhodesia and held high-level talks with Muzorewa in June 1979. In the weeks before the 1981 general election, he faced hard-line Afrikaner hecklers, some supporters of the Herstigte Nasionale Party, resisting changes to apartheid. On the final night of the campaign, he vowed that "As long as there is a National Party Government, we won't hand over South-West Africa to the authority of SWAPO." His party won 58% of the all-white vote and 131 seats, down from 65% and 134 seats in 1977, losing ground to the Herstigte Nasionale Party. In April 1981, Desmond Tutu's passport was seized after he visited Europe and the United States to call for economic pressure on South Africa; Botha was angered and had vowed to seize Tutu's passport. In the same year, he authorized Operation Beanbag, a series of raids by the SADF against safe houses of uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK), the armed wing of the ANC in Mozambique. In February 1982, he survived a leadership challenge from Andries Treurnicht, securing 172 votes to 36 on a motion of support. On 22 April 1983, Botha announced a special commission to consider repealing the Immorality Act and the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act, 1949, stating: "I am personally opposed to immoral practices, but the Government does not see these two laws as guarantees for the survival of South Africa." On 19 May 1983, the International Press Institute issued resolutions condemning the "continued harassment and persecution" of the media in South Africa, appealing to Botha to accept press freedom as a prerequisite for being part of the democratic world and citing difficulties for foreign journalists obtaining visas, as well as the upcoming trials of journalists Allister Sparks, his wife Suzanne, and Bernard Simon, which were dropped in March 1984. In May 1983, he condemned the Church Street, Pretoria bombing by uMkhonto weSizwe, calling it evidence of a "Communist-inspired onslaught." In 1983, Botha proposed a new constitution, put to a vote of the white population on 2 November, which was endorsed by the white electorate. Though it did not implement a federal system, it introduced a power-sharing arrangement with Coloureds and Indians by creating two new houses of parliament—the House of Representatives for Coloureds and the House of Delegates for Indians—alongside the existing white-only House of Assembly. Each chamber had sole jurisdiction over matters relating to their communities, and legislation on "general affairs" such as foreign policy and race relations had to pass all three chambers after joint committee review. White South Africans outnumbered Coloureds and Indians together, preserving white dominance. The plan included no representation for the black majority, allocating each Black ethno-linguistic group a 'homeland' initially as a semi-autonomous area, with blacks legally considered citizens of the Bantustans, not of South Africa, and expected to exercise political rights there. Bantustans were to gradually move toward independence, with sovereign nation status as the final goal. During Botha's tenure, Ciskei, Bophutatswana, and Venda achieved nominal sovereignty and nationhood, recognized only by each other and South Africa, and remained economically dependent. Over half of the Bantustans, notably KwaZulu led by Mangosuthu Buthelezi, rejected independence due to their leaders' opposition to apartheid. The new constitution changed the executive branch from a parliamentary system to a presidential system, abolishing the prime minister's office and merging its functions with the state president, who became an executive with sweeping powers. The president was elected by an electoral college composed of members from the three chambers, not by universal suffrage. The state president and cabinet had sole jurisdiction over "general affairs," and disputes were resolved by the President's Council, composed of members from the three chambers and members directly appointed by the president. In practice, the composition of the electoral college and President's Council made it impossible for Coloured and Indian chambers to outvote the white chamber, even if they voted as a bloc, so real power remained in white hands and in Botha's National Party, which held a large majority in the white chamber due to the first-past-the-post system. Only the challenge from the Conservative Party, which opposed the reforms due to fears of apartheid breaking up, questioned Botha's position. The new constitution was criticized by the black majority for failing to grant them any formal role in government, with the African National Congress and Chief Buthelezi among its opponents, supported by many Coloured, white, and Indian groups including the Progressive Federal Party. International commentators such as the Reagan Administration praised it as a "first step" in a series of reforms. On 14 September 1984, Botha was elected as the first executive State President under the new constitution. Implementing the presidential system was a key step in consolidating his personal power, having previously passed strict laws limiting freedom of speech and frequently declaring states of emergency, including extrajudicial killings by special forces like the Koevoet. In many Western countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Commonwealth, there was debate over imposing economic sanctions to weaken Botha and undermine the white regime. By the late 1980s, as foreign investment declined, disinvestment significantly affected South Africa's economy. After suffering a stroke in 1989, Botha resigned as Leader of the National Party and later as State President, and was succeeded by F. W. de Klerk. After resigning as State President, Botha remained influential in South African politics, opposing de Klerk's reforms, particularly the negotiations to dismantle apartheid and the unbanning of the ANC, and advocating for a no vote in the 1992 referendum. He became a vocal critic of the move toward democracy, maintaining his belief in the necessity of apartheid. In the late 1990s, he faced legal challenges related to his role in apartheid-era policies, notably during Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearings, where he was called to account but refused to fully cooperate. His health declined, and he died on 31 October 2006, at the age of 90.

International commentators, such as the Reagan Administration, praised the reforms as a "first step" in a series of anticipated changes. On 14 September 1984, Botha was elected as the first state president under the newly approved constitution, a move seen as a key step in consolidating his personal power. In prior years, he had passed strict laws limiting freedom of speech and frequently declared states of emergency, which included extrajudicial killings during riots or by special forces like Koevoet. In Western countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Commonwealth, there was significant debate over imposing economic sanctions to weaken Botha and undermine the white regime; by the late 1980s, as foreign investment declined, disinvestment severely affected South Africa’s economy. Botha’s loss of influence was directly linked to decisions at the Reagan/Gorbachev summit in Moscow (29 May – 1 June 1988), which aimed to resolve the Namibia issue, as foreign minister Pik Botha stated it was destabilizing the region and "seriously complicating" South Africa’s own challenges. Soviet military aid would cease and Cuban troops would be withdrawn from Angola once South Africa complied with UN Security Council Resolution 435 by ending its control of Namibia and allowing UN-supervised elections. The Tripartite Agreement, implementing these decisions, was signed at UN headquarters in New York on 22 December 1988 by Angola, Cuba, and South Africa. On 18 January 1989, Botha (aged 73) suffered a mild stroke, preventing him from attending a meeting with Namibian leaders on 20 January; he was replaced by acting president J. Christiaan Heunis. On 2 February 1989, Botha resigned as leader of the National Party, anticipating that his nominee, finance minister Barend du Plessis, would succeed him; instead, the party’s parliamentary caucus elected education minister F. W. de Klerk, who quickly consolidated his position as a reformist, while hardliners supported Botha. In March 1989, the NP elected de Klerk as state president, but Botha refused to resign, claiming constitutional entitlement to remain until March 1990 and even considering a five-year re-election. After acrimonious meetings in Cape Town and following the implementation of UNSCR 435 in Namibia on 1 April 1989, Botha and de Klerk reached a compromise: Botha would retire after the parliamentary elections in September, allowing de Klerk to assume the presidency. However, Botha abruptly resigned from the state presidency on 14 August 1989, citing lack of consultation by de Klerk regarding his visit to Zambia’s President Kenneth Kaunda. De Klerk was sworn in as acting state president on 14 August 1989 and was subsequently nominated by the electoral college for a five-year term. De Klerk quickly removed legislation against anti-apartheid groups, including the African National Congress, and released Nelson Mandela. His term led to the dismantling of apartheid and negotiations culminating in South Africa’s first racially inclusive democratic elections on 27 April 1994. In a 2006 statement on Botha’s death, de Klerk acknowledged that Botha introduced some changes to apartheid, including legalizing interracial marriage and miscegenation, lifting the constitutional ban on multiracial political parties, and relaxing the Group Areas Act by creating "Open Group Areas" – racially mixed neighborhoods requiring government permits, local white support, and being located in upper-class areas of major cities. In 1983, constitutional reforms granted limited political rights to "Coloureds" and "Indians," and Botha became the first South African leader to authorize contact with Nelson Mandela. Despite these reforms, NP hardliners, led by Andries Treurnicht, rejected them, with the group splitting in 1982 to form the Conservative Party, which failed to meet opposition demands. Facing rising discontent and violence, Botha refused to transfer power to blacks and imposed stricter security measures against anti-apartheid activists, refusing to negotiate with the ANC. In 1985, Botha delivered the Rubicon speech, refusing to yield to black demands, including Mandela’s release. His defiance isolated South Africa, leading to economic sanctions and a sharp decline in the rand. The following year, when the United States passed the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act, Botha declared a nationwide state of emergency and famously stated, "This uprising will bring out the beast in us." As sanctions and diplomatic pressure increased, civil unrest spread among the black population, supported by the ANC and neighboring black-majority governments. On 16 May 1986, Botha warned neighboring states against "unsolicited interference" in South Africa’s affairs; four days later, he ordered air strikes against targets in Lusaka, Harare, and Gaborone, including ANC exiled activists, claiming these were a "first installment" showing South Africa’s capacity and will to dismantle the ANC. Despite concessions, Botha’s rule remained repressive: thousands were detained without trial, tortured, or killed. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) found Botha responsible for gross human rights violations and directly authorized unlawful activities, including killings. He declined to apologize for apartheid and, in a 2006 birthday interview, claimed he had no regrets about his leadership. He denied holding black South Africans in inferiority to whites but admitted that "some" whites did; he also stated that apartheid laws originated in Lord Milner’s time and that the National Party merely inherited them, though he conceded that the Afrikaner population had been "happy to perpetuate [apartheid]" as many were, and some still were, "racists at heart." Botha and his wife Elize retired to Die Anker, a home 16 kilometers (9.9 miles) from George on the Indian Ocean coast of the Western Cape. Elize died in 1997 from a heart attack. He was briefly engaged to Reinette Water Naude, 31 years his junior, but on 22 June 1998 married Barbara Robertson, 25 years his junior. Botha remained largely out of the public eye and was widely believed to oppose de Klerk’s reforms; he resigned from the Afrikaner Broederbond. President Nelson Mandela arranged a dinner with Botha’s daughters, Rozanne and Elsa, and their husbands, hoping to persuade them to have their father testify at the TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. There was no consensus within the family, with Rozanne strongly opposing, fearing prosecution or humiliation. The TRC found Botha responsible for the 1988 bombing of the South African Council of Churches headquarters in Johannesburg. In August 1998, he was fined and given a suspended jail sentence for refusing to testify on human rights violations and violence sanctioned by the State Security Council (SSC), which he directed as president until 1989. In June 1999, Botha successfully appealed to the High Court, with Judge Selikowitz (and Judge Foxcroft concurring) ruling that the notice to appear before the TRC was technically invalid. Botha died of natural causes on 31 October 2006, at age 90, at his home in Wilderness. His death was met with magnanimity by many former opponents, with Mandela stating that while Botha remained a symbol of apartheid, he also contributed to the peaceful settlement of the country. President Thabo Mbeki announced flags would be flown at half-mast and a state funeral offered, though the family declined the state funeral and a private one was held on 8 November in George, where Botha was buried. Mbeki attended. However, the government’s decision to honor Botha with official gestures drew public criticism, with organizations like the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) and COSATU opposing it, arguing that a man widely seen as a symbol of apartheid oppression should not receive national recognition.
